Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. For a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, the other threat items describe hypervigilance and startle around other people, and the triggers/memory/appraisal items do not suggest a home-intrusion or boundary-violation danger theme. Repeated door/window checking points to a specific safety behavior focused on securing the environment, which is not supported elsewhere in the selected items and does not fit the formulation well, especially given that maladaptive-strategy links are inactive.

vignette:
Pita is a 71-year-old married man from a Pacific Islander family who has spent the last several years working as a cashier at a neighborhood grocery store. He came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was "not right anymore," though when pressed he struggled to say exactly what had happened. The trauma he circles around occurred outside that same store late one afternoon, when he witnessed a young mother and her baby caught in a violent assault near the entrance. He remembers the baby's crying first, sharp and panicked, and the sudden slam of the automatic outer door as customers rushed in and out. After that, the scene breaks apart for him. He can recall flashes of people moving too fast, the mother on the ground, someone shouting for help, but whenever he tries to put the event into order he loses the thread and stops, saying there are pieces missing and that he cannot make it into a full story even in his own mind.

In the weeks afterward, the sounds and sensations that belonged to that moment began to stand out with a force he could not control. A baby crying in the store, the heavy swing of the stockroom door, even the simple discomfort of feeling hemmed in at his register could make his whole body tense before he had time to think. At work he would jerk when someone stepped suddenly into his peripheral vision, and he found himself scanning customers' hands, faces, and movements as if danger were about to break out again. What frightened him was not only the intensity of his reaction but how quickly it took over; the cry of an infant or the crack of a door seemed to place him back inside an atmosphere where harm could happen at any second.

Those same moments also revived what he had come to believe about the aftermath. Each time the door slammed or a baby cried nearby, he was pulled back not only toward the scene but toward the bitter conviction that the people who should have protected that woman and child had failed them, and that no one had truly been held to account. The more firmly he held that conclusion, the more insistently the scene returned in jagged images, as if his mind kept dragging him back to the mother on the ground and the crying baby to confirm that this was what the world was really like. He speaks with contained anger about how little seemed to happen afterward, how authorities and the systems around them did not provide the safety he had assumed existed. The triggers do not stay as mere reminders; they bring with them the meaning he has made of the event, that ordinary people are left exposed and those responsible often face nothing.

Over time Pita has become increasingly watchful. In line at the store, he studies customers for signs they may turn unpredictable. If someone reaches suddenly for a wallet or shifts a bag too quickly, he startles hard and has to steady himself against the counter. Living in that constant state of alarm has only strengthened his belief that safety is fragile and that people in authority do not truly protect anyone; the fear itself feels like evidence that he was wrong ever to trust that they would. Beneath this is a settled belief that protection cannot be counted on, and that because others failed before, he has to be the one who stays on guard now. That belief keeps his attention fixed outward, always checking, always braced, as though vigilance were the only thing standing between another helpless scene and catastrophe.

His inability to form a coherent account has deepened these convictions rather than softened them. Because the memory comes in fragments, with whole sections missing, the event remains unresolved in his mind, something unfinished and uncontained. He says that if he could remember it straight through, maybe he could understand it, but instead the blanks leave him with a sense that something terrible happened in a world where no one stepped in as they should have. The more broken the memory feels, the more certain he becomes that what happened was intolerable and unforgiven; and that certainty, in turn, makes it even harder for him to stay with the memory long enough to narrate it clearly.

The fragmentation also makes his environment feel studded with warning signals. Because he cannot place the event into a complete past, babies' cries and doors opening or slamming do not feel like neutral present-day sounds. They arrive charged, as if they contain the missing parts of what he still cannot grasp. Even a vague sense of discomfort in his body can act like a cue that something is wrong, and once cued he begins scanning the room, tracking movement and watching people closely for threat.

At home his wife has noticed how emotionally flat he has become. He sits through dinner silent, looking beyond the table, and says he feels dead inside. Yet under that numbness is an angry, mistrustful alertness that has reshaped his days. At the register he asks coworkers to handle families with crying infants when he can, and he positions himself to keep the entrance in sight. What finally brought him in was a recent incident when a child began wailing near the checkout just as the front door slammed behind a customer; Pita spun toward the sound, heart pounding, certain for a moment that someone was about to be hurt. Later he could not explain to his wife why it affected him so strongly, only that the same old certainty returned: people are not protected, no one answers for it, and he is tired of living as if danger is always one sudden movement away. He says he wants help making sense of what happened, but what he fears most is that if he stops watching, the world will prove him right again.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show Pita’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the trauma memory within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not clearly state that his sense of threat leads to or reinforces his negative appraisals within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show Pita’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the trauma memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that his sense of threat leads to or reinforces his negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
